These automated systems play an essential role in maintaining safe operational conditions and minimizing the scope of environmental or operational hazards . LNG production involves substantial power demands, which are critically relevant when considering its use in aviation fuel supply chains. Typical baseload LNG liquefaction plants exhibit a specific energy consumption on the order of 0.25–0.4 kWh per kilogram of LNG (IEA Greenhouse Gas R&D Programme 2019), with about 0.3 kWh/kg used as a representative value. Large-capacity liquefiers generally achieve higher efficiency due to economies of scale and more 58 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. advanced mixed refrigerant or cascade cycle designs, while older or small-scale plants often exhibit higher specific energy consumption approaching 500 kWh/tonne of LNG (Casey 2024). 4.1.4 General Liquified Natural Gas Distribution Methods LNG delivery technologies require a range of specialized equipment due to their cryogenic nature. Vessels, terminals, and processes to transport natural gas in its supercooled liquid state— usually at about −162°C (113 K) from production sites to the end-use markets—demand special infrastructure. Because the liquefied state occupies 1/600 of the volume of its gaseous phase, from an economic point of view, LNG is cheaper to transport over long distances by means other than pipelines. The LNG supply chains are engineered to maintain cryogenic temperatures, ensuring safety and preserving efficiency from the liquefaction plant right through to the regasification facility (Figure 38). Figure 38. Overview of LNG supply chain. Source: Machfudiyanto et al. (2025) The main elements of LNG supply chains are LNG carriers: purpose-built ships designed to transport LNG across the oceans. They utilize either membrane-type containment systems or spherical Moss-type tanks, each with certain advantages as seen in Figure 39. Membrane systems rely on thin, flexible metal membranes supported by insulation layers; such a design allows for the maximum cargo-carrying capacity and efficient general hull design. Moss systems utilize self-supporting aluminum alloy spheres that boast exceptional structural integrity and safety, but at the expense of somewhat reduced cargo space. Modern LNG carrier vessels also have propulsion systems such as dual-fuel diesel engines capable of burning the boil-off gas, thereby increasing the overall efficiency and reducing emissions. 59 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. (2019) LNG loading and unloading requires complicated terminal infrastructure and precision engineering. Export terminals have large-scale liquefaction plants where natural gas is purified, chilled to cryogenic temperatures, and liquefied before being pumped into storage tanks. Such tanks are most often of full-containment design, utilizing reinforced concrete with steel inner shells to store cryogenic liquids safely.
